(InStyle.com) -- Style-maker, TV host and opinionated fashionista Carson Kressley explains how to give yourself a complete makeover--inside and out. Style-maker Carson Kressley spills the naked truth on giving yourself a mental makeover. Minimize the negative . As Coco Chanel said, "Fashion is architecture: It's a matter of proportions." In other words: No matter which part of your body you dislike, there's a clever way to divert the eye elsewhere. Try different styles and employ horizontal (widening), vertical (elongating) and diagonal (slimming) lines as necessary. Venture out of your comfort zone . "Many women get used to dressing their body a certain way because they think it's the only thing that works for them," says Kressley. Find a boutique or department store with well-trained salespeople and try on three styles you've never worn. It might be a fabric such as jersey that you've always deemed too clingy or an Empire-waist camisole that you're convinced looks too young. Not every experiment will be a success, but even one new style or color will prove that there are more ways than you thought to look your best. Don't be ruled by your insecurities . If you've been avoiding the beach or missing out on parties because you're afraid of being the largest person there, grab a friend and go to the very place that incites terror--just be sure you're wearing an amazing outfit. Avoid a blackout . "Have you ever seen a happy goth?" muses Kressley. "I think everyone needs color to feel good." Too many women rely on head-to-toe black as a form of camouflage. But any hue can be slimming if worn monochromatically--so instead of black, reach for plum, gray or chocolate brown. Clean out your closet . Whether you're holding on to clothes that are too small because you hope you'll fit into them someday, or clothes that are too big for fear you'll grow back into them, you're keeping past wounds open. "Old clothes stop you from living in the present," says Kressley. "They reinforce what you used to look like." Get rid of anything you haven't worn in two years and replace it with something new that makes you feel pretty. And while you're out shopping, have a house-cleaner swing by for good measure. Write yourself a love note . Some women are so obsessed with their hips that they fail to notice their flat tummy. Remind yourself of your virtues by writing a note that says something like "Hey, you have a great chest!" Tack it to the bathroom mirror so you'll see it in the morning and before bedtime. "We're so trained to look for the negative that we need a physical reminder of the positive," explains Kressley. Have a princess moment . Treating yourself to a massage, a body exfoliation, a professional blow-out, a brow shaping or a mani-pedi can elevate your mood by affirming to yourself that you're worth the splurge. Get naked . Some women on Kressley's show are so self-conscious about their bodies that they're reluctant to be naked around their husbands. That discomfort affects how they feel when dressed too. Before you can move as if you own the room, you'll have to be at ease inside your skin, and spending time in the buff can help. One idea: Take a bath with the (gasp!) lights on--no candles. "Feeling comfortable with your body alone is the first step to feeling comfortable with your body around others," says Kressley. If all else fails, fake it . One of Kressley's favorite mantras is "looking cute is feeling cute." So if you're having a low day, force yourself to go through the motions. Put on your makeup, do your hair, wear a great outfit. Sometimes faking it can give you enough of a boost to lift you out of the doldrums. "Feeling pretty," Kressley says, "changes your whole outlook because you feel good about yourself." (InStyle.com) -- Style-maker, TV host, and opinionated fashionista Carson Kressley explains how to give yourself a complete makeover—inside and out.

Style-maker Carson Kressley shares the naked truth about giving yourself a mental makeover.

**Minimize the negative.** As Coco Chanel once said, “Fashion is architecture: It’s a matter of proportions.” In other words, no matter which part of your body you dislike, there is a clever way to divert the eye elsewhere. Try different styles, and use horizontal lines to widen, vertical lines to elongate, and diagonal lines to slim as needed.

**Venture out of your comfort zone.** “Many women get used to dressing their body a certain way because they think it’s the only thing that works for them,” says Kressley. Find a boutique or department store with well-trained salespeople, and try on three styles you’ve never worn before. It might be a fabric such as jersey that you have always considered too clingy, or an Empire-waist camisole that you are convinced looks too young. Not every experiment will succeed, but even one new style or color will prove that there are more ways than you may have thought to look your best.

**Don’t be ruled by your insecurities.** If you have been avoiding the beach or missing out on parties because you are afraid of being the largest person there, grab a friend and go to the very place that incites terror—just be sure you are wearing an amazing outfit.

**Avoid a blackout.** “Have you ever seen a happy goth?” Kressley muses. “I think everyone needs color to feel good.” Too many women rely on head-to-toe black as a form of camouflage. But any hue can be slimming if worn monochromatically, so instead of black, reach for plum, gray, or chocolate brown.

**Clean out your closet.** Whether you are holding on to clothes that are too small because you hope you will fit into them someday, or clothes that are too big because you fear you may grow back into them, you are keeping past wounds open. “Old clothes stop you from living in the present,” says Kressley. “They reinforce what you used to look like.” Get rid of anything you have not worn in two years, and replace it with something new that makes you feel pretty. And while you are out shopping, have a house cleaner swing by for good measure.

**Write yourself a love note.** Some women are so focused on their hips that they fail to notice their flat tummy. Remind yourself of your virtues by writing a note that says something like, “Hey, you have a great chest!” Tack it to the bathroom mirror so you will see it in the morning and before bedtime. “We’re so trained to look for the negative that we need a physical reminder of the positive,” Kressley explains.

**Have a princess moment.** Treating yourself to a massage, body exfoliation, professional blowout, brow shaping, or mani-pedi can elevate your mood by affirming that you are worth the splurge.

**Get naked.** Some women on Kressley’s show are so self-conscious about their bodies that they are reluctant to be naked around their husbands. That discomfort affects how they feel when dressed, too. Before you can move as if you own the room, you have to be at ease in your own skin, and spending time in the buff can help. One idea: Take a bath with the—gasp!—lights on, and no candles. “Feeling comfortable with your body alone is the first step to feeling comfortable with your body around others,” says Kressley.

**If all else fails, fake it.** One of Kressley’s favorite mantras is, “Looking cute is feeling cute.” So if you are having a low day, force yourself to go through the motions. Put on your makeup, do your hair, and wear a great outfit. Sometimes faking it can give you enough of a boost to lift you out of the doldrums. “Feeling pretty,” Kressley says, “changes your whole outlook because you feel good about yourself.”

outputs.L2:
(InStyle.com) — Carson Kressley—style expert, television personality and outspoken fashion commentator—shares advice for transforming yourself both emotionally and physically. The fashion authority offers a candid guide to refreshing your mindset as well as your look.

**Play down what bothers you.**  
Coco Chanel once said, “Fashion is architecture: It’s a matter of proportions.” Put another way, whatever area of your body you feel unhappy with, clothing can help shift attention somewhere else. Experiment with silhouettes, and use lines strategically: horizontal lines can add width, vertical ones can lengthen, and diagonal lines can create a slimming effect.

**Step beyond familiar territory.**  
“A lot of women become accustomed to dressing their bodies in one specific way because they believe it’s the only approach that suits them,” Kressley says. Visit a boutique or department store with knowledgeable sales associates and try on three looks you’ve never considered before. Maybe it’s jersey, a fabric you’ve always thought would cling too much, or an Empire-waist camisole you assumed would look too youthful. Some attempts may not work, but discovering even one new shade or silhouette can show you that you have more flattering options than you realized.

**Don’t let self-doubt make your decisions.**  
If fear of being the biggest person at the beach or at a party has kept you from going, bring a friend and face the place that makes you anxious—while wearing an outfit that makes you feel fantastic.

**Don’t disappear into black.**  
“Have you ever seen a happy goth?” Kressley wonders. “I think everyone needs color to feel good.” Many women use all-black outfits as a kind of disguise. But dressing in one color from head to toe can be flattering in many shades, not just black. Try plum, gray or chocolate brown instead.

**Edit your wardrobe.**  
Keeping clothes that are too small because you hope to wear them again someday—or holding on to oversized pieces because you worry you might need them later—can keep old insecurities alive. “Old clothes stop you from living in the present,” Kressley says. “They reinforce what you used to look like.” Donate or discard anything you haven’t worn in two years, and buy something new that makes you feel attractive. While you’re shopping, he suggests going one step further and having a house cleaner come by.

**Leave yourself a compliment.**  
Some women focus so intensely on one feature, like their hips, that they overlook something they like, such as a flat stomach. Give yourself a reminder by writing a note along the lines of, “Hey, you have a great chest!” and placing it on your bathroom mirror, where you’ll see it in the morning and at night. “We’re so trained to look for the negative that we need a physical reminder of the positive,” Kressley explains.

**Give yourself a princess-worthy treat.**  
A massage, body scrub, salon blow-out, eyebrow shaping or manicure-pedicure can improve your mood because it sends the message that you deserve the indulgence.

**Spend time unclothed.**  
On Kressley’s show, some women feel so uneasy about their bodies that they hesitate to be naked even in front of their husbands. That discomfort can influence how they feel in clothes as well. To carry yourself confidently, you first need to feel comfortable in your own skin, and being nude can help. One suggestion: take a bath with the lights on—no candles. “Feeling comfortable with your body alone is the first step to feeling comfortable with your body around others,” Kressley says.

**When nothing else works, pretend until it feels real.**  
One of Kressley’s favorite sayings is, “looking cute is feeling cute.” If you’re having a bad day, go through the routine anyway: apply makeup, style your hair and put on an outfit you love. Acting confident can sometimes create enough of a lift to pull you out of a slump. “Feeling pretty,” Kressley says, “changes your whole outlook because you feel good about yourself.”

Carson Kressley advises people to reduce negative focus on their bodies by using fashion strategically. Rather than concentrating on areas they feel insecure about, he recommends choosing clothing with proportions, shapes, and lines that draw attention to their most flattering features. The right cut, silhouette, or detail can help shift focus and create a more confident overall appearance.

He also encourages women to experiment with styles, fabrics, and colors outside their usual comfort zones. Trying something new can be a powerful way to discover unexpected looks that are both flattering and enjoyable. A different texture, a brighter color, or a fresh silhouette may help someone see themselves in a new and more positive way.

Kressley believes insecurities should not stop people from participating in life. Whether it is going to a party, attending a social event, or enjoying an activity, people should not hold themselves back because of how they feel about their bodies. When someone is wearing an outfit that makes them feel confident and polished, they are more likely to relax and enjoy the experience.

He also recommends moving beyond an all-black wardrobe. While black can be flattering and easy to wear, relying on it too much can limit personal style. Instead, Kressley suggests trying other monochromatic colors, such as plum, gray, or chocolate brown. These shades can still create a streamlined, elegant look while adding warmth, interest, and variety.

Finally, Kressley advises people to clean out old clothes that no longer fit. Keeping these items can keep a person emotionally tied to the past, especially if the clothes represent a former size or stage of life. Letting them go makes room for clothing that fits well now and supports confidence in the present.

Carson Kressley approaches personal makeovers as more than a change of clothes. For him, style is a practical way to help women see themselves differently, feel more confident, and let go of old ideas about what they can or cannot wear. His advice combines fashion strategy with emotional encouragement, reminding women that the goal is not perfection but a more honest, comfortable, and expressive version of themselves.

A major part of his approach is learning how to work with the body rather than fight against it. Kressley encourages women to stop focusing only on what they consider flaws and instead use clothing to create balance and proportion. The right fit, shape, and silhouette can draw attention to favorite features while making areas of insecurity feel less noticeable. Rather than hiding under oversized or outdated clothing, he suggests choosing pieces that fit well and make the wearer feel polished and present.

He also urges women to experiment with styles they might normally avoid. Many people limit themselves because they have decided, often years earlier, that certain cuts, colors, or trends are “not for them.” Kressley challenges this thinking by encouraging women to try unfamiliar clothing with an open mind. A new neckline, a different pant shape, a more defined waist, or a bolder accessory can reveal possibilities that someone may never have considered. Trying something new does not mean abandoning personal taste; it means expanding it.

Color is another important part of his makeover philosophy. Kressley sees color as a powerful tool for lifting mood and changing the way a person presents herself to the world. While neutral clothing can be useful, relying on it too heavily can sometimes reflect caution or self-protection. Adding color—whether through a dress, jacket, scarf, shoe, or lipstick—can bring energy, warmth, and personality into an outfit. It can also help a woman feel more visible in a positive way.

At the same time, Kressley recognizes that makeovers often involve deeper insecurities. Clothing can carry emotional weight: a dress saved for a body someone used to have, jeans kept as a reminder of a past size, or garments worn simply because they feel safe. He encourages women to clear out clothes that reinforce shame, regret, or limitation. A closet should support the person someone is now, not punish her for changing or keep her trapped in the past.

His message is ultimately about freedom. By experimenting with proportion, fit, color, and attitude, women can begin to see style as a source of possibility rather than pressure. Looking better is not just about impressing others; it is about feeling at home in one’s body and life. Kressley’s makeover advice suggests that when women stop dressing for fear and start dressing for confidence, they can use fashion as a tool for self-acceptance, self-expression, and living more fully in the present.

# Carson Kressley’s Confidence-Boosting Style Tips Are the Wardrobe Reset We All Need

Carson Kressley has built a career on one deceptively simple idea: great style isn’t about having a “perfect” body, a massive budget, or a closet full of designer labels. It’s about learning how to show up for yourself — with a little polish, a little playfulness, and a whole lot of self-acceptance.

The fashion expert, TV personality, and longtime champion of feel-good dressing has always approached style as something bigger than clothes. The right outfit can change your posture. A great jacket can make you walk differently. A bold color can shift your mood before you’ve even left the house.

If your closet has been feeling more stressful than inspiring lately, consider this your permission slip to reset. Below, Kressley-inspired tips for improving body confidence and developing personal style that feels authentic, flattering, and fun.

## 1. Dress the Body You Have Today

One of the biggest style traps is waiting: waiting to lose weight, waiting for a different season of life, waiting for the “right” occasion. But confidence starts when you stop treating your current body like a temporary problem.

Instead of saving style for some future version of yourself, build a wardrobe that supports you now. That means buying clothes that fit comfortably, tailoring pieces when needed, and letting go of anything that makes you feel punished by your own closet.

A too-tight pair of jeans or a dress that requires constant adjusting is not motivation — it’s a mood killer. Clothes should work for you, not the other way around.

## 2. Fit Is Everything

The most expensive outfit in the world won’t look chic if the fit is off. On the flip side, a simple blazer, white shirt, or pair of trousers can look incredibly polished when the proportions are right.

Pay attention to shoulder seams, waist placement, hem length, and how a garment moves when you sit, walk, or raise your arms. If something almost works, a good tailor can be your secret weapon. Shortening a sleeve, nipping in a waist, or adjusting a hem can make a piece feel custom.

The goal isn’t to hide your body. It’s to let your clothes frame it beautifully.

## 3. Find Your “Style Anchors”

Personal style can feel overwhelming if you think you need to reinvent yourself every season. A better approach: identify a few style anchors — the pieces, colors, or silhouettes that consistently make you feel like yourself.

Maybe it’s a sharp blazer, a printed scarf, a great boot, wide-leg denim, statement glasses, or a signature color. These anchors become your fashion home base. From there, you can experiment without feeling lost.

Think of it as building a style vocabulary. Once you know your favorite words, getting dressed becomes much easier.

## 4. Use Color Strategically

Black will always be chic, but color has serious confidence-boosting power. A saturated jewel tone, a crisp white, a warm camel, or even a pop of pink can brighten your complexion and your mood.

If you’re color-shy, start small. Try a vibrant handbag, a colorful flat, a printed blouse under a neutral blazer, or a swipe of lipstick that makes your whole outfit feel intentional.

The point isn’t to wear every trend. It’s to notice what makes you light up.

## 5. Balance Proportions, Don’t Obsess Over Size

Stylish dressing is less about the number on a tag and more about proportion. If you’re wearing something voluminous on top, try a slimmer shape on the bottom. If you love wide-leg pants, pair them with a more defined top. If a dress feels shapeless, add a belt or cropped jacket to create structure.

These little styling choices can help an outfit feel pulled together without making body confidence about shrinking yourself.

And remember: sizing is wildly inconsistent. A number is information, not an identity.

## 6. Create Outfits, Not Just a Closet Full of Clothes

A common reason people feel like they have “nothing to wear” is because they own individual pieces, not complete looks. Spend an hour creating outfit formulas you can rely on.

Try combinations like:

- Blazer + tee + straight-leg jeans + loafers  
- Midi dress + denim jacket + ankle boots  
- Button-down shirt + wide-leg trousers + statement earrings  
- Monochrome knit set + sleek sneakers  
- Pencil skirt + soft sweater + pointed flats  

Take mirror selfies of outfits you love so you can revisit them on busy mornings. Confidence often comes from preparation.

## 7. Add One “Joy Piece”

Every wardrobe needs practicality — but it also needs delight. A joy piece is something that makes you smile the second you put it on. Maybe it’s a sequined top, a leopard-print coat, metallic shoes, a dramatic necklace, or a fabulous pair of sunglasses.

You don’t need a special event to wear something fun. In fact, the everyday outfit is often exactly where a joy piece belongs.

Style should have a little wink.

## 8. Stop Saving the Good Stuff

The “good” perfume, the beautiful coat, the fancy earrings, the silk blouse — wear them. Life is not improved by keeping your favorite things hidden in a closet.

When you use your best pieces in real life, you send yourself a subtle message: I am worth the effort today.

That mindset may be the most stylish thing of all.

## 9. Edit Without Guilt

A confidence-building closet is one that reflects who you are now. If something no longer fits, feels dated in a way you don’t enjoy, carries a bad memory, or simply never gets worn, it may be time to let it go.

Editing your wardrobe isn’t wasteful when done thoughtfully. Donate, resell, tailor, or pass pieces along. What remains should make getting dressed feel easier, not emotionally complicated.

A great closet gives you options — not anxiety.

## 10. Let Compliments In

Body confidence isn’t built overnight. It grows through small choices: wearing the outfit, standing tall, accepting the compliment instead of deflecting it.

The next time someone says, “You look great,” resist the urge to explain, minimize, or point out what you don’t like. Just say, “Thank you.”

It sounds simple, but it’s powerful.

## The Carson Kressley Takeaway

The best personal style doesn’t come from chasing trends or dressing for approval. It comes from curiosity, self-knowledge, and a willingness to have a little fun in front of the mirror.

Wear the color. Tailor the jacket. Buy the jeans that fit. Put on the sunglasses. Stop waiting for permission.

Confidence isn’t about looking like someone else — it’s about finally dressing like yourself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
